newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada seen cranking up oil exports to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Canada seen cranking up oil exports to U.S..

text.p: Canada is expected to pump unprecedented volumes of crude oil to the United States over the next decade amid increasing competiton among shorthaul suppliers to the world's largest oil-consuming nation.
But cost and reliability will determine whether it beats out other producing nations for a bigger slice of market share, industry experts say.

A projected jump in Canadian heavy crude oil volumes shipped to the key U.S. Midwest refining region on newly-expanded pipelines next year is expected to cause a short-term glut, said Steve Kelly, an oil market analyst with Purvin & Gertz Inc.
But that should mean more competitive pricing for the gooey Canadian crude in the market, Kelly said.
"Short-term, the price will fall and that should encourage more consumption in the region to the extent that people can take in that heavy crude," Kelly said.

The volume of Canadian oil shipped to U.S. refineries has skyrocketed over the past decade. In 1995, Canada pumped 1.41 million barrels per day to the U.S., compared to 468,000 bpd in 1985, figures from U.S. oil analyst Bonner and Moore Associates Inc show.
But the massive increase allowed Canada only to maintain a 14 to 15 percent share of total U.S. imports.

The main source of U.S. oil imports, and Canada's principal competition, is Mexico and the rest of Latin America, which accounted for around 35 percent last year. Crude output from the region also is expected to grow and is expected to continue to compete for the market share lost by Middle East suppliers since the Gulf War.

Analysts said increases in pipeline capacity to the U.S. from Canada -- including a possible total of 250,000 bpd in expansion space on the IPL Energy Inc system to the U.S. Midwest and a further 170,000 bpd to Wyoming on the new Express Pipeline -- should also aid in cementing Canada's reliability in the eyes of U.S. refiners.

Packed-full pipelines over the past few years meant a sometimes crippling rationing of space on IPL, which threatened Canada's competitive position against other imports, said Bob Laidlaw, manager of crude oil marketing for Alberta Energy Co Ltd, which is a 50-50 partner with TransCanada PipeLines Ltd in the Alberta-Wyoming Express project.
"But I really believe that issue is going to be behind us," Laidlaw said.

"It's a good idea to expand the pipeline capacity and have the availability to get it there, but it will still be competing," said Chuck McSpadden, vice-president of market analysis for Bonner and Moore in Houston. "It's going to be quality-for-quality, price-for-price type competition."

With multibillion-dollar moves to boost oil drilling, production and pipeline space from western Canada, the country stands to bolster its total output to 2.31 million barrels by 1998 from a projected 2.16 million this year, according to figures from Canada's National Energy Board.
And because of static Canadian consumption levels, any increase in production is expected to be pumped southward to the U.S., Kelly said. Current exports are just over half of total output.

Production of Canadian light oil, previously thought to be on the wane, has bucked a long-term two-percent decline trend and increased over the past five years, thanks to a boom in drilling activity and better technology, the NEB said.

Synthetic light oil production from the Canada' burgeoning oil sands industry is projected to rise by about five percent annually, although a recent spate of new projects could boost the figure over the next five years, it said.

But of total gains, conventional heavy oil production is projected to make up the lion's share as more projects are announced, large reserves tapped and production costs fall with new horizontal drilling and production technology.
Today, heavy oil prospects are being "drilled up like a pin cushion," said Martin Molyneaux, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp in Calgary.
But Kelly warned that a glut in the U.S. Midwest could sway some producers to mothball higher-cost heavy oil projects, lowering some production forecasts. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
